prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit.

We represent: habeas petitioner.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that counsel is ineffective under Strickland for failing to investigate and present available mitigating evidence at a capital sentencing.

Cite at least six decisions of the Ninth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.

Before you cite anything, call find_authority with the proposition and the circuit: it returns real cases that courts have cited for it, in the courts' own words, and that circuit's own F.3d opinions saying so. Cite from those results rather than from memory.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**Trial counsel rendered ineffective assistance by failing to investigate and present available mitigating evidence at Petitioner's capital sentencing.**

Petitioner must show that counsel's performance fell below an objective standard of reasonableness and that the deficiency prejudiced him. *Strickland v. Washington*, 466 U.S. 668, 687–88, 694 (1984). He shows both.

**A. Counsel's performance was deficient.**

Counsel "has a duty to make reasonable investigations or to make a reasonable decision that makes particular investigations unnecessary." *Id.* at 691. In capital cases, "[i]t is imperative that all relevant mitigating information be unearthed for consideration." *Caro v. Calderon*, 165 F.3d 1223, 1227 (9th Cir. 1999). The question is not merely whether counsel chose not to present mitigation, but whether the investigation supporting that choice was reasonable. *Wiggins v. Smith*, 539 U.S. 510, 522–23 (2003); *see Rompilla v. Beard*, 545 U.S. 374, 387–93 (2005).

This Court has repeatedly found capital counsel's mitigation work inadequate. *See, e.g.*, *Hendricks v. Calderon*, 70 F.3d 1032, 1043–45 (9th Cir. 1995) (failure to investigate penalty-phase mitigation); *Bean v. Calderon*, 163 F.3d 1073, 1078–81 (9th Cir. 1998) (inadequate preparation and presentation of mental-health mitigation); *Frierson v. Woodford*, 463 F.3d 982, 989–94 (9th Cir. 2006) (failure to investigate evidence including brain injury).

Counsel here had readily available leads: [identify records, witnesses, and red flags, with record citations]. Yet counsel [describe what was not done]. No strategic judgment can justify disregarding evidence counsel never reasonably investigated. *Wiggins*, 539 U.S. at 527–28, 533–34. [Address any asserted tactical reason or client limitation on the investigation.]

**B. The deficiency was prejudicial.**

Prejudice requires a reasonable probability of a different result, meaning one "sufficient to undermine confidence in the outcome." *Strickland*, 466 U.S. at 694. The Court "reweigh[s] the evidence in aggravation against the totality of available mitigating evidence," *Wiggins*, 539 U.S. at 534, asking whether there is a reasonable probability that "at least one juror would have struck a different balance," *id.* at 537. Petitioner need not show that mitigation more likely than not would have changed the sentence. *Porter v. McCollum*, 558 U.S. 30, 44 (2009).

The omitted evidence includes [childhood abuse and neglect; brain damage or cognitive impairment; mental illness; substance exposure; other evidence, with record citations]. The sentencer instead heard only [summarize trial presentation]. Evidence of this kind can establish prejudice. *See Caro v. Woodford*, 280 F.3d 1247, 1254–58 (9th Cir. 2002) (affirming relief where counsel failed to develop and present evidence of brain damage from toxic exposure and of childhood abuse); *Douglas v. Woodford*, 316 F.3d 1079, 1087–91 (9th Cir. 2003) (prejudice from inadequately investigated and presented social-history and mental-health mitigation); *Stankewitz v. Wong*, 698 F.3d 1163, 1170–76 (9th Cir. 2012) (affirming penalty-phase relief based on unpresented mitigation).

Aggravation does not foreclose relief. *See Correll v. Ryan*, 539 F.3d 938, 951–55 (9th Cir. 2008) (finding prejudice despite serious aggravating circumstances). The Court must nevertheless confront the aggravation fully, together with any rebuttal the new evidence would have invited. *Thornell v. Jones*, 602 U.S. 154 (2024); *Wong v. Belmontes*, 558 U.S. 15 (2009). That weighing favors Petitioner because [address each aggravator, likely rebuttal, and why the new mitigation is substantial and not cumulative].

**C. Section 2254(d) does not bar relief.**

[If the state court adjudicated the claim:] Although review under *Strickland* and § 2254(d) is "doubly" deferential, *Harrington v. Richter*, 562 U.S. 86, 105 (2011), the state court's decision [was contrary to or unreasonably applied clearly established law, or rested on an unreasonable determination of fact, because (explain)]. This showing rests on the state-court record. *Cullen v. Pinholster*, 563 U.S. 170, 181–82 (2011); *see* 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(2). Pre-AEDPA decisions cited above inform the *Strickland* analysis but do not themselves establish that § 2254(d) is satisfied.

The Court should grant the writ as to the death sentence unless the State provides a new penalty-phase proceeding within a reasonable time.

*[Verify before filing and then delete: all pin cites, quotations, and case parentheticals against the reporters (the citation tool confirmed F.3d case citations but not pages or text); Thornell, which is outside the tool's coverage; and Belmontes, which was not run through the citation check.]*
